The First House, Rochester
images/loc_rochesterFirstHome.svg

PLACEHOLDER: 1986 to 1991, the first house, in Rochester NH — the one with the porch you could see the river from. In 1991 you started kindergarten at Jack and Jill, in a yellow coat you refused to take off.
Start kindergarten at Jack and Jill
true
normal
PLACEHOLDER: four years old, and the teacher says your name back to you.
Hide behind the coat rack until the second bell
penalty
PLACEHOLDER: it works for eleven minutes.
Say your name to everyone in the room, twice
heal
PLACEHOLDER: the room says it back. Something settles.
St. Elizabeth Seton School
images/loc_stElizabethSeton.svg

PLACEHOLDER: kindergarten and first grade at St. Elizabeth Seton, still in Rochester. Two rooms, one teacher who knew your name and your mother's, and a walk to the church that you insisted on doing backwards.
Walk to school backwards the whole way
true
normal
PLACEHOLDER: it takes twice as long, and you still get there first.
Move to a school further from home
penalty
PLACEHOLDER: a longer drive, and nobody to sit with.
Learn the names of everyone in both rooms
heal
PLACEHOLDER: first grade ends with thirty names and nobody missing.
The Move to Strafford
images/loc_theMoveToStrafford.jpg
PLACEHOLDER: 1993. Rochester to Strafford, in a car with more boxes than seats. Strafford Elementary from kindergarten all the way through eighth grade — the longest address you ever had.
Unpack the box marked KEEP FIRST
true
normal
PLACEHOLDER: books, the good blanket, the tape player. First night, first order of business.
Unpack the box marked THROW AWAY FIRST
penalty
PLACEHOLDER: you break something irreplaceable before the first school day.
Introduce yourself to a neighbour before you unpack
heal
PLACEHOLDER: by Sunday you have a house key that is not yours.
The Strafford Elementary Talent Show
images/loc_theTalentShow.jpg
It's time to show off your talent at the Strafford Elementary School. How will you impress your classmates?
Grab the microphone and pretend you're on Delilah, belting out "Wind Beneath My Wings.”
true
normal
You did Bette Midler proud.
Kart wheel across the carpet during circle time, showing off your new gymnastics moves.
penalty
Oompf. That hurt. Maybe you should have grabbed a microphone instead.
Recite your favorite Shel Silverstein poem from memory.
heal
If only talent shows were this wholesome.
The DARE Graduation
images/loc_theDareSpeech.jpg
Sixth-grade DARE graduation: how will you promote a drug-free life?
Deliver a graduation speech to save your classmates from becoming future addicts.
true
normal
Words have power. Thanks for keeping these kids pure.
Doodle new logos for DARE in your class notebook that end up on their website.
penalty
Pay attention, kid, and get your head out of your notebook.
Wear your DARE-themed t-shirt at graduation creating a viral fashion trend in your middle school.
heal
Hey, the lead singer of Bloc Party had a DARE t-shirt, but you wore it first.
The Piscataqua Youth Players
images/loc_piscataquaYouthPlayers.jpg
Piscataqua Youth Players: Stage fright or stage might?
Shoot for the stars and take the lead role as the Velveteen Rabbit in the titular play.
true
normal
The playbill says so. So does VHS recording of your performance.
Skip the stage and use your artistic talents to create the set for the Velveteen Rabbit.
penalty
You were made for the lime light, my dear.
A rabbbit? You sat this one out and played Lucy Oopma Loompa in Charlie and the Chocolate Factory instead.
heal
You rose the occasion and did both. A true rising star.
Disney World, Jellystone, Poland Springs
images/loc_theFamilyTrips.svg

PLACEHOLDER: the three places you asked to go back to. Disney World in Orlando, Jellystone Campground in New Hampshire, and your grandparents' camp at Poland Springs, Maine — same camp, same rock, every summer for years.
Swim at Jellystone every single morning
true
normal
PLACEHOLDER: the water is cold, and you were in it before breakfast. Every day.
Ride the biggest one at Disney World, twice
normal
PLACEHOLDER: twice, because the first time you were too small to remember it.
Go back to the same spot at Poland Springs every year
heal
PLACEHOLDER: the same rock, the same view, the same people already waiting.
Destination Imagination, First Place
images/loc_destinationImagination.svg

PLACEHOLDER: March 2000. Your Destination Imagination team took first place, and you were three hundred miles away at your brother's hockey tournament in Pennsylvania. Train from Philadelphia to Boston, bus to Portsmouth, Aunt Lynne waiting at Kingswood High School in Wolfeboro. You flew back for the rest of the tournament and were told at the rink. There is a newspaper article.
Take the train, then the bus, to get there in time
true
normal
PLACEHOLDER: Philadelphia to Boston to Portsmouth, and Aunt Lynne at the school gates. You make it.
Stay at the tournament and miss it
penalty
PLACEHOLDER: you hear about first place in a car park, a week later, out of somebody else's newspaper.
Carry the trophy home down the aisle yourself
heal
PLACEHOLDER: trophy on your lap, Portland to Philadelphia. Nobody says a word the whole way.
"Stories Are Made That Way"
images/loc_storiesAreMadeThatWay.jpg
PLACEHOLDER: 1 April 2002. The musical CD comes out, and you sing several of the tracks with the other children. You still have the CD.
Sing your own tracks, not only the backing
true
normal
PLACEHOLDER: several songs, with the other children, on an actual record.
Sing backing vocals only
penalty
PLACEHOLDER: you are on every track, and nobody would know it from the sleeve notes.
Learn every other child's part as well
heal
PLACEHOLDER: you could have sung any of them. You never needed to.
Washington DC, July 2003
images/loc_theLeadershipConference.svg

PLACEHOLDER: the teaching staff at Bishop Brady nominated you for the National Student Leadership Conference in Washington DC, in the area of Business and Commerce. July 2003: you went. There is a letter.
Go to Washington DC that July
true
normal
PLACEHOLDER: nominated by the teaching staff, in Business and Commerce. The letter is real.
Skip it — there was a tournament that summer
penalty
PLACEHOLDER: you were at the rink. The letter stays in a drawer.
Take notes on everyone you met
heal
PLACEHOLDER: you came home with a notebook and no idea what you wanted yet.
Editor's Choice, Achievement in Poetry
images/loc_editorsChoicePoetry.svg
PLACEHOLDER: March 2004. The Editor's Choice Award for Achievement in Poetry. There is a certificate, which means somebody wrote your name on a line and meant it.
Accept the poetry award
true
normal
PLACEHOLDER: Editor's Choice, Achievement in Poetry, March 2004. The certificate is signed.
Turn it down — you were only doing it for the class
penalty
PLACEHOLDER: you give it back, the class gives it back, and it ends up in a drawer either way.
Read one poem out loud at the ceremony
heal
PLACEHOLDER: your own, not the one that won. It goes over well.
Singing the National Anthem, June 2005
images/loc_theNationalAnthem.jpg
PLACEHOLDER: June 2005, Bishop Brady High School graduation. You sang the National Anthem. Nobody who loves you knew you were going to do it.
Take the microphone at graduation
true
normal
PLACEHOLDER: a surprise to everyone who loves you, which is most of why it worked.
Let somebody else do it
penalty
PLACEHOLDER: it goes well. You spent the whole thing on the sideline.
Sing it looking at one person you trust
heal
PLACEHOLDER: one person. The rest of the stadium is a blur afterwards.
Stonehill to Emerson
images/loc_stonehillToEmerson.jpg
Stonehill College in Janurary 2007: is your higher education high enough?
Transfer to Emerson College and major in the lucrative craft of poetry.
true
normal
Let's transform the mundane together and write a senior thesis.
Stay at Stonehill. Why fix what ain't broke?
penalty
Everything was broken. Not even Jesus could fix it.
Turn-down a full ride to Boston University and take a gap year.
heal
Universities just mean smaller fish in a bigger pond.
Magna Cum Laude
images/loc_magnaCumLaude.jpg
PLACEHOLDER: you graduated from Emerson, Magna Cum Laude, with a BFA in creative writing and a concentration in creative non-fiction and poetry. Both halves of it, in one degree.
Put creative non-fiction and poetry in the same degree
true
normal
PLACEHOLDER: BFA, creative writing, concentrated in creative non-fiction and poetry. Magna Cum Laude.
Choose one and drop the other
penalty
PLACEHOLDER: you take the practical half. The other one keeps. It does not go anywhere.
Thank the teachers who wrote you a reference
heal
PLACEHOLDER: you kept the emails. You use them later, more than once.
WEGO Health, Somerville
images/loc_wegoHealth.svg

PLACEHOLDER: April 2012, Somerville. Health Social Media writer at WEGO Health, and an advocate for Patient Leaders — the company that empowers health activists to help other people. Your article, "Patient Leaders of Online Health Communities Discuss Patient to Patient Conversations on Clinical Trials", ran in Monitor Magazine, the global voice of clinical research professionals. There is a copy of the magazine.
Write about patient leaders, for patient leaders
true
normal
PLACEHOLDER: April 2012, Somerville. The Monitor article. There is a copy of the magazine.
Write the press release instead
penalty
PLACEHOLDER: it goes out. Nobody has to think about it, which was never the point.
Let a patient leader read it before it runs
heal
PLACEHOLDER: they change two sentences. Both of them are better.
Spindrift, and Watertown
images/loc_spindrift.jpg
PLACEHOLDER: 2017, twice over. You started working at Spindrift Beverage Company, and later the same year you moved to Watertown, Massachusetts.
Take the job at Spindrift, and move to Watertown
true
normal
PLACEHOLDER: a new job, and a new town later in the same year. Both of them 2017.
Turn the offer down and stay where you are
penalty
PLACEHOLDER: the offer goes to somebody else. So, more or less, does Watertown.
Take the job and commute from where you already live
heal
PLACEHOLDER: you keep the postcode you know, and learn the job twice as fast.
Belmont, 2020
images/loc_belmontFamily.svg
PLACEHOLDER: 2020. You started a family, and moved to Belmont, Massachusetts.
Start a family, and move to Belmont
true
normal
PLACEHOLDER: 2020, two enormous things at once, and a new postcode to learn on the way.
Wait a year, and do one thing at a time
penalty
PLACEHOLDER: the year goes differently. Belmont happens without you.
Move first, and let the rest follow
heal
PLACEHOLDER: you learn the town while there is nothing else on your mind.
The Fourth Decade

PLACEHOLDER: forty, and the road still going. Every stop on it is yours: the first house in Rochester, a yellow coat, a talent show on somebody's video tape, a train from Philadelphia, a cake with the candles knocked over on the ground, and a great deal of work done on behalf of other people. The Oracle puts the book away.
PLACEHOLDER: forty, with a coin left at the shrine out of habit. Somebody has to move the shrine before the next traveller gets there. You do it yourself, and it is very funny.

The journey ends
PLACEHOLDER: three stumbles and the Oracle calls it. She recommends rest, tea, and a second attempt — the whole of it is still there, exactly where you left it.
